To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the hydraulic and biochemical traits of plants are linked through the steady‐state coupled carbon and water transport model and that the model predicts the decline in maximum carboxylation rate ( V cmax ), as the soil‐plant hydraulic capacity decreases, which is consistent with the observed patterns of V cmax with stand development or plant age.

(i) the steady-state analytical model provides a simple, yet robust, framework to understand the relationship between hydraulic and biochemical properties in plants; (ii) the relationship between V cmax and soil‐plant hydraulics is consistent with measurements from different forest types; and (iii) V cmax declines with stand age or development as a function of soil‐plant hydric properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between hydraulic and biochemical properties in plants.
the evolution of plant hydraulic and biochemical traits in relation to plant water supply.
the development of a theoretical framework for linking hydraulic and biochemical plant properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is consistent with the data.
the hydraulic and biochemical characteristics of plants are linked by the demand‐supply equilibrium of water and carbon.
the hydraulic and biochemical characteristics of plant species are not necessarily linked, but that they can be linked by the steady-state coupled water and carbon flux model.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the biochemical capacity for photosynthesis is a function of plant hydraulic properties and that these properties are linked through stomatal control of water loss.
the hydraulic and biochemical components of the model are linked by the steady‐state constraint imposed on the balance of water supply and demand in the soil‐plant‐atmosphere system.
hydraulic and biochemical properties in plants are linked by the requirement for water supply to meet the demand for CO2 by photosynthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydraulic and biochemical traits are coupled by the demand for CO2 in the leaf.
the hydraulic properties of the soil‐plant‐atmosphere system constrain the biochemical properties of plants, which in turn constrain the hydraulics of the soil‐leaf system.
the hydraulic properties of a plant stand can constrain the biochemical properties of its individual trees.
